 Birth Rates Are Down. Give Party Dads a Chance.
 By 
 Sarah Wheeler ,
 'Mother of it All' podcast co-host & 'Momspreading' newsletter author.   
 She also writes the parenting column "Good Enough Parent," and has written about parenting, culture, and neurodiversity for Romper, Salon, HuffPost, The New York Times, and more. She has a PhD in educational psychology from the University of California, Berkeley. 
 Nov. 13, 2026 
 Save this article to read it later.
 Find this story in your account’s ‘Saved for Later’ section.
 Photo: A24/Courtesy Everett Collection 
 You’ve probably heard that young Americans are experiencing an unparalleled parenting crisis. The surgeon general declared parenting a nationwide health emergency. Birth rates have steadily declined for two decades. Sam Altman thinks AI chatbots should prep kids for their days on the drive to school .
 In the midst of all this comes Jordan Firstman ’s filmmaking debut, Club Kid , a laugh-a-minute, cry-into-your-popcorn banger of a movie that is small in scale but big in feeling. It makes a strong case for the positive impact of children on the sometimes directionless lives of adults. When queer party promoter Peter learns he made a baby the one time he accidentally slept with a woman (yes, it’s medically possible; yes, it’s a movie), he has to transition quickly from coke on the coffee table to caring for another human — 10-year-old Arlo. Can a wayward gay with a few thousand bucks in his bank account handle the responsibility of a child? Some of Peter’s friends clearly think absolutely not . But what does a child really need from an adult, anyway?
 Many have compared Club Kid to Adam Sandler ’s 1999 movie, Big Daddy , where, in a much more cis, straight world, Sandler’s character adopts a kid to win back the affections of a woman who has deemed him too immature. The plots are eerily similar, but — maybe this is my hetero-pessimism talking — the vibes couldn’t be more different. To use Club Kid ’s parlance, while the film does “give” Big Daddy , it’s more spiritually related to Mike Mills’s tremendous 2021 film, C’mon C’mon , which starred Joaquin Phoenix as a bachelor uncle who gets stuck with his sister’s kid for a while and whose heart grows three sizes in the process.
 As in C’mon C’mon , the chemistry between Firstman’s Peter and the outstanding Reggie Absolom’s Arlo is as palpable as an EDM beat, and the audience finds itself wishing someone would look at us the way these two look at each other. Despite his precocious taste in music (“But I like Björk!”), Arlo is not an unrealistic child. He comes close to but never quite crosses that cringey “Curly Sue” rubicon wherein a magical child turns a bad adult (usually a straight white man) good with sheer pluck and probing truisms. Sure, he is eager to please and strangely comfortable with grown-ups, but many parentified children adopt these traits as a matter of survival. (We learn throughout the film that Arlo’s mother was not capable of keeping him safe, even if she did love him very much.)
 Anyone with children in their lives can feel how grounded the impact of Arlo on Peter truly is in the film. The love he builds is almost painfully tender, like the ache I feel when I watch my daughter’s sleeping face after she has called me the worst mom in the world for making a spicy dinner. I know she doesn’t mean it, that being a child in an adult world is strange and cruel and sacred. “He’s cleaner than me,” Peter says of his son. Cue the tears.
 How does one become a good dad? Peter doesn’t quite seem to know, but loving Arlo lets him love himself, and we watch that growth over the span of a tight two-hour run time in surprisingly authentic beats for a somewhat hackneyed premise (see Big Daddy , above). In one tense scene, Peter is torn about whether to put Arlo in a very adult situation that he and others are counting on. As a parent myself, who wasn’t exactly fucking strangers on “G” when my kids were born but who has grown up considerably over the decade since, it was a revelation to watch Peter learn to define the boundaries that needed to be created between his child and the world, and realizing, not without horror, that he is the one who has to set them. You may hold your breath at this point in the film because you are scared for Arlo, but perhaps also because you are bearing witness to the uneven, messy metamorphosis we humans undergo when tasked with the care of other people.
 Arlo doesn’t judge Peter’s queer community, and they, in turn, don’t judge him. They know how shitty the world can be, and they let him have fun in it, get angry in it, whatever he needs to do. There is no pathologizing here. Besides, plenty of kids growing up in two-parent heterosexual homes have it pretty bad. What could be so horrible about giving a single gay man in active ketamine withdrawal a chance?
 Peter is not alone in his initial confusion around what purpose a child could possibly fill in his life: Published just a few months ago, journalist Anna Louie Sussman’s Inconceivable: The Impossibility of Family in an Age of Uncertainty laid out the endless reasons (family-last policy, crap economy, lack of community) that we don’t want or can’t have kids. In 2024’s What Are Children For? , by philosophers Anastasia Berg and Rachel Wiseman, an entire book is made out of the ambivalence that Millennials and Gen Z have towards child-rearing. Last year’s If I Had Legs I’d Kick You, a very different movie that encapsulated, importantly, the rough side of parenting that elder Millennials have perhaps emphasized too much, was unwatchable for some ( not me !) for this reason. Watching Club Kid , I feared that some viewers might be too uncomfortable with the casual references to Arlo’s past and future trauma, or the precarious situations Peter puts him in (these are not treated casually, though, despite being filled with humor). Sadly, we do live in a society that takes terrible care of children. Over 10 million children in the US live in poverty. One in seven experience abuse or neglect. At least 200,000 have had a parent detained by immigration in the past two years. Club Kid hurts for Arlo, and leads the audience to wish for him to have a parent who has their shit together. But it respects the reality of childhood by not glossing over how hard childhood actually is for most kids.
 Another fall film about the way children can alter the paths of their fathers in interesting new ways is the standout Your Mother Your Mother Your Mother , which stars Mahershala Ali as a hit man named Latif whose wife dies and leaves him to care for his three children while trying to get himself out of a job he doesn’t want to do. Just like Club Kid ’s Peter, the juxtapositions between Latif’s lifestyle and his parenting never get old, and YMYMYM treats us to the most edge-of-your-seat breastfeeding scene you never knew you needed. It’s a premise that is perhaps a tad more far-fetched than a gay man’s onetime vaginal ejaculation turning up a decade later, but great writing and acting (and a jaw-dropping breakout performance from Adia as Latif’s teenage daughter, Fatiha) keep the parent-child relationships grounded.
 There’s some killer swordwork in YMYMYM , but it’s ultimately a story about how the love for your children saves you — from inertia and grief and, most important, yourself. In making YMYMYM , the film’s writer and director, Bassam Tariq, a father of two, wanted to explore what happens when children see the worst parts of their father, the “monster side.” His thesis, in life and in the film, is that as long as you keep showing up authentically for your children, they will love you no matter what. Maybe there are, and should be, a few exceptions to this rule, but despite not considering myself a pro-natalist, I can’t help but pitch this as one of the most powerful reasons to procreate.
 We know what these films think children are for, but what are adults for, especially at a time when it’s hard for them to get jobs or homes, or when a global pandemic fucked the rythm of their young adulthood and they are still stuck six years later? Firstman, 35, hasn’t had children yet, though he did donate sperm for his sister’s partner’s baby, becoming an uncle for the first time on the last day of filming Club Kid. He has said, though, that the process of making this movie forced him to grow up. “I needed to change and I didn’t know how,” he’s told crowds at Club Kid screenings. Luckily for him, he was able to knock out some self-transformation while making a hell of a film. For the rest of us, there’s always parenting.
